introduction-why-databases-are-different.core: Application code is like a whiteboard: wipe it and rewrite it. Databases hold accumulated state that can't be recreated, so changes must be versioned, tested, compatible and forward-only.

first_principles.problem: Teams apply CI/CD to code but still change schemas by hand, which causes drift between environments and risky releases.
derivation: Stay **compatible** with old and new code (expand-contract).

analogy.title: A whiteboard vs. a stone tablet
analogy.story: Mistakes on a whiteboard are erased; carvings in stone are permanent, so you plan every cut.
analogy.breaks: Small, frequent, reversible-by-design changes make database CD practical.

example.title: Manual vs automated schema changes
flow: Manual: staging has index, prod doesn't
Automated: same migrations everywhere in order

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Environments match, and changes are reviewed.

example.outcome: schema changes go through the same pipeline as code.

check.q: Why can't you treat schema changes like code deploys?
check.a: The database holds persistent state, and destructive changes can't be undone by redeploying.

the-expand-contract-pattern-safe-schema-.core: Never make a breaking schema change in one step. Expand (add the new, compatible structure), migrate the code and data, then contract (remove the old) once nothing depends on it.

first_principles.problem: Dropping or renaming a column in the same deploy as the code change crashes old instances still running.
truths: Rolling deploys run old and new code together.
Additive changes don't break old code.
Removal is safe only after every reader is gone.
derivation: **Add** the new column or table (nullable or defaulted).
**Drop** the old one in a later release.

analogy.title: Adding a new door before bricking up the old one
analogy.story: People keep using the old door until the new one is open and familiar.
analogy.breaks: It adds releases and temporary complexity (dual writes).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Zero downtime and no crashing old pods.

check.q: Why add a column as nullable during expand?
check.a: So old code that doesn't write it keeps working.

the-migration-based-approach-imperative.core: Flyway and Liquibase apply ordered, versioned migration scripts (V1__init.sql, V2__add_index.sql) and record what's been applied in a history table, so every environment replays the same sequence.

first_principles.problem: Without an ordered record, nobody knows which changes each database has received.
truths: A history table records the state.
derivation: The tool applies **pending ones in order**.

analogy.title: Turn-by-turn directions
analogy.story: Each step assumes the previous ones were followed, and the log shows how far you've got.
analogy.breaks: Long migration histories get slow to replay from scratch, so use baselines.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every environment converges through the same steps.

code.text:
flyway -url=$DB_URL validate   # checksums match?
flyway -url=$DB_URL migrate    # apply pending V*__*.sql

check.q: What happens if you edit an already-applied Flyway migration?
check.a: The checksum no longer matches, so validation fails.

the-schema-as-code-approach-declarative.core: Declarative tools like Atlas take the desired schema (HCL or SQL) and compute the diff against the live database to generate the migration plan, the way Terraform does for infrastructure.

first_principles.problem: Hand-writing every migration is tedious, and the current schema is hard to see across 300 migration files.
truths: The desired end state is easier to read than a history.
derivation: Run **atlas schema diff/plan** against the live DB.
**Review** the generated SQL (lint for destructive changes).
**Apply**, or commit the plan as a versioned migration.

analogy.title: Giving a destination vs. turn-by-turn directions
analogy.story: The GPS computes the route from where you are.
analogy.breaks: Diff engines can't infer intent: a rename looks like drop plus add, which loses data.

example.title: An Atlas plan with lint

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A destructive diff is blocked for human review.

code.text:
atlas migrate diff add_status --to file://schema.hcl --dev-url docker://postgres/16
atlas migrate lint --latest 1   # flags: dropping column 'state'

example.outcome: readable schemas and generated, linted plans.

check.q: Why can a declarative diff be dangerous for renames?
check.a: It sees a removed column and a new column, generating a drop plus add that loses data.

rollback-strategies-the-myth-of-undo.core: Database rollbacks rarely restore reality: new data has been written since. Prefer roll-forward fixes, backward-compatible changes (so code can roll back independently), and backups or PITR for disasters.

first_principles.problem: A 'down' migration drops a new column that already holds a day of customer data.
truths: Data written after the change has to be preserved.
Code rollback is easy when the schema stays compatible.
Backups are the true last resort.
derivation: Design changes so **old code still works** (expand-contract).

analogy.title: Un-baking a cake
analogy.story: You can't remove eggs from a baked cake; you bake a better one next time.
analogy.breaks: Some trivial changes (adding an unused index) can be safely reversed.

example.title: A bad release with a new column
flow: v2 adds column + code using it
Roll back code to v1 (column ignored)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No data lost and a quick recovery.

check.q: Why are down migrations risky in production?
check.a: They can destroy data written since the migration ran.
